Week 7 · Module 8 · five days · about 6 hours in total

This is the week Claude stops answering and starts acting.

Until now you have asked Claude questions and read the replies. In Week 6 you built n8n workflows that ran the same path every time. This week we put the two together. An agent is Claude inside an n8n node, with a memory and a handful of tools, deciding for itself which tool to use next until the job is done. I have cut the week into five days, from 45 minutes to about two hours. By Day 5 you will have built a support agent that looks customers up in a mock CRM and emails the right person, and only when it should.

Day 1 · about 45 minutes

What an agent is, and the node that holds one

Two ideas today. First the loop every agent runs: think, act, observe, repeat. Then the n8n node that runs that loop, with its three sockets. By the end you will have built the smallest possible agent in n8n and watched it reach for a calculator instead of guessing. Every visual on this page is live; poke it.

Step 0 of 14
Goal: "Check my three open tickets and email me about the urgent one." Step through it and count the passes.14 steps · 5 passes

The loop every agent runs

Think about how you handle a request like "check my three open tickets and tell me which one is urgent". You do not answer from memory. You open the ticket system, read the list, open the ones that look serious, and only then write back. Each step depends on what the last one showed you. That is the shape of an agent's work, and it is why a plain chat reply cannot do it: a chat reply is one pass, and this job takes several.

Here is the loop. Claude reads the goal and thinks: can I answer now, or do I need something first? If it needs something, it acts, by writing the name of a tool and the inputs for it as a small JSON object. It does not run the tool. n8n runs the node and hands the result back. Claude observes the result and thinks again. Round and round, until it decides it has enough and writes a final answer. People in the trade call this think, act, observe; you will also hear "reasoning and acting". Same idea.

Step through the simulator on the left. The ticket job takes five passes: one to list the tickets, two to open the suspicious ones, one to send the email, one to write the reply. "What are your opening hours?" takes a single pass, because nothing needs looking up. You do not fix the number of passes. The model decides as it goes, and that is exactly what makes this an agent rather than the Week 6 workflow where you drew every arrow yourself.

Where the picture breaks. Claude is not sitting there waiting between passes. Each pass is a fresh request to the model with the whole conversation so far, every tool result included, pasted in again. The "memory" between passes is text, and you pay for it in tokens every time. That is why a twenty-pass agent is expensive, and why Day 4 caps the loop.

An agent is a model in a loop: think, act, observe, repeat, until it writes a final answer. The model chooses the path. n8n runs the tools.

One node, three sockets

In Week 6 every node did one job and you drew the path between them. The AI Agent node is different. Drop it on the canvas and three sockets hang underneath, labelled Chat Model, Memory and Tool. The node itself is the loop from the last concept. What you plug into the sockets decides what the loop can do.

The Chat Model socket takes exactly one sub-node, and for us that is the Anthropic Chat Model. You attach your API key as an n8n credential, never typed into the node itself, and pick a model from the list. Use claude-sonnet-5-5 for this course: quick enough for a chat, reliable at choosing tools. claude-haiku-5-5 is cheaper for high-volume routing and claude-opus-5-5 is for decisions where a wrong call is expensive. Model names change every few months; the syllabus this course grew from still says Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Pick whatever the current Sonnet-class model is called on the day you build.

The Memory socket takes a memory sub-node, which keeps recent messages so the agent can follow a conversation; that is tomorrow's first concept. The Tool socket takes as many tools as you like: a Calculator, Gmail, Google Sheets, an HTTP Request, even a whole other workflow. Each one appears to Claude as a name and a description it may choose to call. Plug things in on the left and read the line under the node. It tells you what that agent can and cannot do.

One honest note on names. n8n renames things between versions. The memory node was called Window Buffer Memory for a long time and is now Simple Memory; the Tool socket has been labelled Tools. The jobs of the three sockets have not changed, so when a label on your screen differs from this page, look for the job, not the word.

The AI Agent node is the loop. Chat Model is the brain, Memory is what it remembers, Tool is what it can do. The key lives in a credential.

Day 2 · about 55 minutes

Memory, and the words that steer a tool

Today is about the two things that most often go wrong in a first agent: it forgets what you told it, or it reaches for the wrong tool. By the end you will know exactly what a memory window keeps, you will have rewritten a tool description until the agent behaves, and you will have run a real Claude agent in the Agent Playground.

Sent to the model this turn: 0 of 0 messagesabout 0 tokens
Greyed-out messages are on your screen but not in the request. Add turns until the introduction falls out, then read the reply.remembers the name

What a memory window actually keeps

Picture a colleague who covers your support chat but works under a strict rule: before answering each message, they may read only the last ten messages in the thread, nothing older. Most of the time nobody notices. Then a customer writes "as I said at the start, my name is Priya", and the colleague has no idea who Priya is. That rule is a memory window, and it is exactly what the memory sub-node gives your agent.

Here is the thing that confuses almost everyone the first time. The chat on your screen shows the whole conversation. The model sees none of it unless it is sent again. Every pass of the loop is a fresh request, and the memory node decides how many past messages get pasted into that request. Set the window to ten and the agent "remembers" ten messages. Set it to one and it sees only what you just typed.

Why not keep everything? Because every message you keep is tokens you pay for on every pass, and because the context window from Week 1 is finite. A support agent handling a hundred chats a day with full history would be slow and expensive for no benefit; nobody needs the opening pleasantry from forty messages ago. The window is a budget. Slide it on the left, add turns, and watch which messages fall out of view. Then read what the agent says when asked its customer's name.

Two things the window does not do. It does not survive a new session: tomorrow's chat starts empty unless you store something yourself, which is Week 9's topic. And it does not hold tool results from earlier turns unless they were written into the conversation, so an agent that looked a customer up ten messages ago may need to look them up again. That second lookup is cheap. Guessing instead is not.

Memory is the last N messages pasted into every pass. The screen shows everything; the model sees only the window.

send_alert: "Send email"
Right decisions out of six. Illustrative: a real model is less tidy, but the pattern holds.0 / 6

The agent decides from the description alone

Imagine handing a new temp a desk phone with a sticky note that says "phone". They know what it does. They do not know when you want them to use it, who to call, or what to say. So they either never touch it or they call the finance director about a stapler. A tool description is that sticky note, and Claude is the temp. It reads the description at the moment it decides, and that is all it has.

So a description has four parts. What the tool does. When to use it. When not to use it. And what each input means, in plain words, with the shape it expects. "Send email" fails on three of the four. "Email the customer's account manager. Use only when the customer reports an outage or asks to cancel. Never use for general questions. Inputs: to (the manager's email from lookup_customer), subject (short), body (under 100 words)." answers all four and is still short enough to read in one breath.

Run the tester on the left with each version. With "Send email" the agent alerts the account manager about opening hours, because nothing told it not to. The half description fixes some messages and not others. The full one gets all six. In my experience this is where half of all agent debugging happens: not in the model, not in the workflow, but in the words of the description. When your agent misbehaves, read the description first and ask whether a temp would have done the same.

An honest caveat. A good description lowers wrong calls; it does not make them impossible. The model is still predicting, and an ambiguous message ("I might cancel if this keeps up") can go either way. Day 4 adds a second layer, rules in the system prompt, and the lab adds the third: a test table you fill in.

A description says what, when, when not, and what each input means. The agent decides from those words alone.

Day 3 · about 60 minutes

Data out, and tools that reach outside n8n

Three ideas today, all about the edges of the agent. How to make its final answer data instead of prose, how to give it a whole workflow as a tool, and how to let it call any system on the web with the HTTP Request tool. By the end your agent will return a tidy JSON object and will have fetched something real from outside n8n.

// schema the next node expects
{ "customer": string, "action_taken": string, "needs_followup": boolean }
The final answer appears here.
Validator: waiting
Message: "This is Priya Nair, the site is down." Ask in both modes and watch the validator.three fields, typed

When the next node needs fields, not a paragraph

Think about what happens after the agent. In a real workflow its answer is rarely the end. Something has to log the case to a sheet, set a priority flag, or decide whether a person should look. Those nodes cannot read "I looked up Priya and emailed her manager, someone will follow up". They need customer, action_taken and needs_followup, each in its own field, each of the right type.

That is what an output parser does. You attach a Structured Output Parser to the agent, give it a schema (the fields you want and their types), and switch on "Require specific output format" in the node. The agent is now told to answer in that shape, and n8n checks the result against the schema. If a field is missing, or a boolean comes back as the word "maybe", the parser can send the answer back to the model to fix. Press the button on the left in both modes and watch the validator do its job.

Two cautions. A schema is a contract, so keep it small: three to six fields the next node really uses, no more. And do not confuse this with the tools' inputs. Tools also take structured data, but that is Claude filling in a tool's form during the loop. The parser is about the final answer, after the loop ends. Week 8 goes deeper into schemas when you write tool definitions by hand in the Console.

Prose is for people. A Structured Output Parser makes the final answer a fixed data shape the next node can read, and n8n validates it.

0 wrong calls in 10
Two narrow tools with one verb each. Every call lands where it should.

A whole workflow can be a tool

At work you do not do everything yourself. You pass the invoice question to accounts payable and the contract clause to legal, and you trust each to come back with an answer. An agent can work the same way. In n8n, any workflow that starts with an Execute Workflow trigger can be attached under the agent's Tool socket with the Call n8n Workflow Tool. To Claude it looks like any other tool: a name, a description, a few inputs. Behind it there can be twenty nodes.

This is how you build specialists. A lookup workflow that reads the CRM, cleans the row and returns only the fields that matter. A writing workflow that drafts and formats an email in the company style. Each one can be tested on its own, pinned, versioned and reused by other agents, and the main agent stays small and readable. The diagram on the left shows the shape: one main agent, two narrow tools, every call landing where it should.

Now switch the diagram to one wide tool. A single "do_customer_stuff" workflow that looks up, updates, emails and refunds has to be described in one paragraph, and the agent then guesses which part it is triggering. Wrong calls follow, and some of them change records. The rule I use: one tool, one verb. If you cannot describe a tool in two sentences, split it.

The Call n8n Workflow Tool turns any workflow into a tool. Keep each one narrow: one tool, one verb.

Reaching any system on the web

        
Most of what your company runs has an address that programs can talk to: the CRM, the ticketing system, the carrier that ships your parcels, the bank's exchange-rate feed. That interface is called a REST API, and it works the way your browser does. You send a request to a URL, usually with a few headers (an API key, the format you want), and you get JSON back. In Week 6 you watched JSON move between nodes. This is the same JSON arriving from outside.

        
The HTTP Request tool hands that ability to the agent. You set the method and the URL, add any headers, and write a description. The agent decides when to call it and what to put in the parameters. The JSON that comes back becomes the observe step of the loop. Pick an endpoint on the left and send a request, then read the line at the bottom: out of a response with hundreds of values, the agent needs one or two.

        
Three habits keep this safe. Put the API key in an n8n credential, not in the URL, so it never appears in a log. Prefer GET requests for a first agent; a tool that can POST can change records, and you want to decide deliberately which of those you allow. And trim the response: the tool's own options or a Set node can cut a 400-line reply down to the three fields the agent needs, which saves tokens and stops the model being distracted by the rest.

        
Where it breaks. An API can be down, slow, or changed since you built the tool. Give the agent a rule for what to say when a tool returns an error, and set the node to continue on failure with an error branch, exactly as you did in Week 6.

        
The HTTP Request tool lets the agent call any REST API. Keys in credentials, GET before POST, trim what comes back.

      Day 4 · about 75 minutes
      
Standing orders, and reading a run that went wrong

      
Tomorrow you build the lab agent. Today you learn the two skills that make it work first time: writing the standing orders in the system prompt, and reading an execution log to see which part to fix. By the end you will have drafted the system prompt you will paste into the lab.

    

    
    

      

        

          

            
            
            
            
            
          

          

          

        

        
Untick a rule, or drop Max Iterations to 3, and see which message was quietly relying on it.0 / 6 handled well

      

      

        
The system prompt is the agent's standing orders

        
A good team lead does not brief a new hire on every ticket. They give standing orders once: always check the account before promising anything; escalate outages to the duty manager; never promise a refund over a certain amount without sign-off. After that, the hire decides case by case. The AI Agent node has a place for exactly this, the system message in its options. Everything Week 2 taught you about structured prompts applies here, with one difference: these rules are about which tool to use, and when.

        
The rules I give a triage agent are short, and you can read them on the left. Always call lookup_customer before deciding anything about a customer. Call send_alert only for an outage or a cancellation threat. Never send an alert for a general question. If the customer is not in the CRM, say so and ask for the name on the account. After acting, tell the customer exactly what you did. Untick each rule in turn and run the six messages. You will see which message each rule was quietly protecting.

        
One more setting in the node belongs with the rules: Max Iterations, the ceiling on how many passes the loop may run before n8n stops it. The default is ten. Set it too low and a legitimate multi-step job stops half done, as the last message in the tester shows. Leave it very high and a confused agent can go round forty times at your expense. Ten is a sensible place to start for a support agent.

        
Rules and descriptions overlap on purpose. The description tells the model what a tool is for at the moment it looks at that tool. The system prompt tells it how to behave across the whole conversation. When both say "never alert for a general question", you get far fewer misfires than with either alone.

        
The system prompt carries the standing orders: which tool, when, what to do when a lookup fails, and how to report back. Max Iterations caps the loop.

When it goes wrong, the log tells you which part to fix

        
Every run of an n8n workflow leaves an execution log, and for an agent the log is unusually readable. You can see each pass, the tool it chose, the inputs it filled in, and the result that came back. When a colleague makes a bad call you ask them what they were thinking. With an agent, you can simply read it.

        
Four parts can be at fault, and each leaves a different trace. If the agent called a tool it should not have, or skipped one it should have used, read the tool description first. If it called the right tools in the right order but drew the wrong conclusion, or forgot to say what it did, look at the system prompt. If it lost track of something said earlier in the conversation, that is the memory window. And if it called the right tool with the right inputs and the result was wrong or empty, the tool itself is broken: a sheet column renamed, a filter on the wrong field, a credential that expired.

        
Work through the four runs on the left and pick the part you would fix first. The order matters, because the cheapest fix is usually the right one: a description is one sentence, a system prompt is a paragraph, a tool is a node you have to re-test. Week 8 turns this into a habit called execution monitoring, where every run writes a summary row to a sheet so you can audit a week of decisions in a minute.

        
Wrong tool: the description. Right tools, wrong conclusion: the system prompt. Forgot something: memory. Right call, wrong result: the tool itself.

      Day 5 · about 125 minutes
      
Decide what stays with people, then build the agent

      
The longest day. One idea from the MIT course about where an agent's intelligence ends and a person's begins, then Lab 3.2: a Claude-powered n8n agent that reads a mock CRM and sends Gmail alerts, tested against eight messages. Then design-log entry 7, the quiz and a practice round.

    

    
    

      

        
Agreement with my allocation – / 8
sort all eight

        

        

        
Eight decisions from the triage workflow. For each, who should make it: the agent, the agent proposing with a person deciding, or a person only?from MIT xPRO, Module 6

      

      

        
From humans in the loop to computers in the group

        
Think about the support team your agent is joining. It is not one person at one screen. It is a group: a triage lead, account managers, someone on call, a finance person who signs off refunds. The MIT xPRO course this week borrows from, Designing and Building AI Products and Services, spends a module on what its instructor, Thomas Malone, calls superminds: groups of people acting together in ways that seem intelligent. His argument is that almost everything we have achieved was done by such groups, and that the useful question about AI is not "people or computers" but what people and computers can do together.

        
The distinction that makes this practical is between two kinds of intelligence. Specialised intelligence achieves specific goals in a particular environment; general intelligence achieves a wide range of goals across many environments. The course's example is IBM's Watson, which beat the best human Jeopardy players and could not play noughts and crosses. A five-year-old has more general intelligence than any computer, and human-level general AI, Malone notes, has been "about twenty years away" for the last sixty. So every use of computers has to involve people. His slogan: move from humans in the loop, one person checking one computer, to computers in the group, where the computer does the specialised parts it does better and the people keep everything else.

        
For your agent this is a design decision, not a philosophy. Looking up a record, classifying a message, drafting a reply, doing arithmetic: specialised, measurable, give it to the agent. Deciding to close a long-standing account, approving a refund over a threshold, judging whether a complaint about tone is fair: general, consequential, keep it with a person and have the agent prepare the case. Sort the eight decisions on the left and compare your allocation with mine. Some are judgement calls, and I say which.

        
One more idea from the same module is worth stealing. Malone describes cyber-human learning loops: the computer watches the decisions people make, learns the pattern, starts suggesting, and once people have accepted its suggestion many times in a row it stops asking. That is a sensible path for an agent at work. Start with the agent proposing and a person approving. Promote a decision to the agent only once a test table like today's shows it gets that decision right. Design-log entry 7 asks you to write this down for your own product.

        
An honest caveat. Malone's examples predate language models, and Claude is far more general than Watson was. The line between specialised and general has moved. The decision has not: an agent should own what it does reliably and measurably, and people should own what carries judgement, consequence or accountability.

        
Computers in the group: give the agent the specialised, measurable work; keep judgement with people; promote a decision to the agent only after the test table says you can.

An agent that reads a mock CRM and sends Gmail alerts

      
You build a support triage agent for Stride Shoes, a pretend online shoe shop. A message arrives, the agent looks the customer up in a mock CRM, and emails the account manager only when the message is an outage or a cancellation threat. A company builds this so that every outage reaches the right person within a minute, without the alert channel filling up with questions about opening hours. Everything here is made up: the customers, the addresses, the company.

    Test the tool on its own first with a name you know is in the sheet. Nine times out of ten the filter is on the wrong column, the sheet name has a stray space, or the header row was not read as a header. This is also the "tool itself" case from Day 4.
    4. 
        
  4. Tool 2, send_alert. A Gmail Tool, operation Send, signed in with the test account. Let the model define To, Subject and Message.
    Description: Email the customer's account manager.
Use only when the customer reports an outage or asks to cancel.
Never use for general questions. Inputs: to (the manager's email from lookup_customer),
subject (short), body (under 100 words).
    5. 
        
  5. The standing orders. Paste your Day 4 draft, or the starting prompt below, into the agent's system message. Role, five rules, tone.
    
          
    Copy a starting system prompt
    <role>You are the support triage agent for Stride Shoes, an online shoe shop.</role>
<rules>
1. Always call lookup_customer before deciding anything about a customer. Ask for the name if you do not have it.
2. Call send_alert only when the customer reports an outage or asks to cancel. Send it to the account manager from the CRM.
3. Never call send_alert for a general question. Answer it instead.
4. If the customer is not in the CRM, say so and ask for the name on the account.
5. After acting, tell the customer exactly what you did and why.
</rules>
<style>Short, calm, friendly. Under 80 words.</style>
    6. 
        
  6. Eight test messages. Send the eight messages in the table below, one chat each: three routine questions, three outage reports, two cancellation threats. After each, open the execution log and write down which tools were called, in what order, with what inputs, and what landed in the test inbox. When you are done the inbox must hold exactly five emails.
    Notice: "correct" means the right tools, in the right order, with the right inputs. A good reply after a wrong tool call is still a fail.
    7. 
        
  7. Break it, then fix it. Change the send_alert description to "Send email" and send the three routine questions again. Count the misfires. Restore a precise description and send them a third time. Record both descriptions in the deliverable box.
    
          
    It did not misfire
    Newer models resist the easy version. Make it harder: also remove rule 3 from the system prompt, or send a routine message with an anxious tone ("I really need this sorted today, what are your hours?"). If it still behaves after three tries, write that down; knowing what the agent reliably gets right is part of the test.
    8. 
        
  8. Hand-in. Export the workflow as JSON from the editor menu (Download), finish the test table, keep both descriptions, and write design-log entry 7 below.
    9.

      Check yourself
      
Eight quick questions

      
Pick an answer to see why it is right or wrong. Score 80 percent or more to pass. Nobody is watching; the point is to find out what did not stick.

    

    

    
Think it through

    

      
Why does the agent need a memory node when the chat trigger already shows the whole conversation?
The chat panel shows the history to you, not to the model. Every pass of the loop is a fresh request, and only what the memory node supplies is sent along with it. Without memory each message arrives alone, so the agent cannot connect "my name is Priya" to "what is my name?" three messages later. The window is also a budget: every kept message is tokens paid for on every pass.

      
A tool description says "Does stuff with customers." What three problems will this cause?
The agent cannot tell when to use it, so it calls it for the wrong requests and skips it for the right ones. It cannot tell what inputs to pass, so inputs arrive empty or invented. And it cannot tell the tool apart from the other customer tools, so when two could fit it picks between them at random. The fix is the four-part description: what, when, when not, and what each input means.

      
Your agent emailed the account manager about opening hours. Which part of the system do you fix first?
The send_alert description, because the model reads it at the moment it decides and the fix is one sentence: "Never use for general questions; answer them instead." Then add the same rule to the system prompt so the two layers agree. Only if it still misfires do you look further, at the memory window or at the tool's own inputs. Cheapest fix first, and re-run the eight tests after every change.

      
Your agent can look customers up and send alerts. Name one decision you would refuse to automate, and say why in the MIT course's terms.
Closing an account because a customer asked to cancel. It is irreversible, it has financial and emotional weight, and someone has to be accountable for it, which makes it general intelligence in Malone's sense, not the specialised kind a computer does better. The agent should still do the specialised part: confirm the request, look up the account, draft the summary, and hand the decision to a person. If the test table later shows the hand-offs are always approved unchanged, you can consider promoting the decision, which is the cyber-human learning loop the course describes.
